title: Lifting the scroll
hook: the open scroll is raised high for everyone to see

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yad, the silver hand. Your line was a hand that points. Today, the scroll leaves the table and goes up.

A person walks up to the reading table and takes hold of the two wooden rollers of an open Torah scroll. It's heavy, and open several columns wide. They slide it to the edge, bend their knees, and in one motion lift it high overhead, arms spread, the letters facing the room. Then they turn slowly, so everyone can see. Some people stretch out a finger toward it. Some sing. Nobody breathes much until it's safely down.
screen: `TWO WOODEN ROLLERS.` → `LIFTED HIGH, ARMS SPREAD.` → `TURNING SO EVERYONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: It's called hagbah, lifting. The lifter raises the scroll open, often wide enough that at least three columns show, and turns so every part of the room can see the writing. A later rabbinic handbook for scribes, tractate Soferim, describes the scroll shown to everyone, men and women, so all could see the letters and bow. As it rises, the congregation sings: this is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel. The first half comes from Deuteronomy. In the old Jewish translation: "And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel." It echoes a much older scene. When Ezra the scribe gathered the people in Jerusalem, the book of Nehemiah says he opened the book in the sight of all the people, "and when he opened it, all the people stood up." The timing differs. In most Ashkenazi communities, the lifting comes after the reading; in most Sephardi communities, before. Then a second person, the golel, rolls the scroll closed and dresses it again in its cover. The Talmud, in Megillah 32a, gives that rolling a surprising honor: the one who rolls the scroll receives the reward of all the readers. So the text isn't just read to people. It's shown: lifted out of the experts' hands and turned toward everyone, so the whole room can see it's real.
screen: `HAGBAH: LIFTING.` · `THIS IS THE TORAH MOSES SET BEFORE US.` · `EZRA OPENED IT; ALL STOOD.` · `ASHKENAZI AFTER, SEPHARDI BEFORE.` · then, large: `LIFT IT UP.`

segments.voice: Think of something you love that other people rarely get to see: a book that changed you, a grandmother's recipe, a song, a skill you're quietly good at. Picture holding it up for one person, not explaining it to death, just turning it toward them so they can see it for themselves.
Hagbah. Lifting. The open Torah scroll raised high and turned so everyone in the room can see the writing.
Your line: lift it up. What's held high is meant for the whole room. Day five hundred ninety-nine, done.

chat.says: Why does someone hold the Torah scroll up over their head at services?
options: So the whole room can see the writing itself, not just hear it read.
To show the scroll's cover and crown before it's put away again.
So only the reader can check the letters before the reading starts.
chat.meaning: In hagbah the open scroll is raised and turned so everyone can see the letters, as Ezra opened the book in the sight of all.
